explanations.answer: Go and present himself to Ahab
explanations.explanation: That's the word. The LORD tells Elijah, the prophet, "Go and present yourself to Ahab…" (1 Kings 18:1). Ahab is Israel's king, and he's the very man Elijah told about the drought (1 Kings 17:1). That's a walk straight into the lion's den, and Elijah just goes. I would have needed a minute and a cookie.

explanations.answer: Hide again by the Brook of Cherith
explanations.explanation: Close, because Elijah did hide there once. Earlier the LORD told him, "Leave here, turn eastward, and hide in the Brook of Cherith" (1 Kings 17:3). This time the word is the opposite. Elijah isn't told to hide, he's told to go present himself to Ahab, Israel's king.

explanations.answer: Stay on with the widow in Zarephath
explanations.explanation: Zarephath is another stop on Elijah's road. The LORD sent him there before, saying, "Go at once to Zarephath of Sidon and stay there" (1 Kings 17:9). But in the third year of the drought, the word is different. Elijah is told to go present himself to Ahab, Israel's king.

Rain! The LORD tells Elijah, "…I will send rain upon the face of the earth." In the third year of the drought, that's the best sentence anybody could hear. Notice who does the sending, too. The LORD says, "…I will send…"

Peace would be nice, but that's not the promise here. The LORD says He will send rain upon the face of the earth. That's a big deal in the third year of a drought. A dry land needs rain, not a greeting card.

Help sounds right, and rain surely would help. But the LORD gets more specific than that. He says, "…I will send rain upon the face of the earth." In the third year of the drought, the promise has a name, and the name is rain.
True. The text says Obadiah "…greatly feared the LORD…" He's in charge of the palace of a king who has turned from the LORD, and he still honors Him. That's a man holding steady in a hard place.

The text says the opposite. Obadiah, the man in charge of Ahab's palace, "…greatly feared the LORD…" You might expect a palace worker under that king to go along with the crowd. Obadiah doesn't, and the next verse shows how.

Cave is right. Obadiah took a hundred prophets and hid them fifty men per cave. He also kept them supplied with food and water. A hundred prophets, two caves, and one busy palace man with a very secret errand.

A house is a fair guess, but the text puts them somewhere else. Obadiah hid the prophets fifty men per cave. He also provided them with food and water. Caves are good for staying out of sight, and I know a thing or two about hiding, since I spent years in the back of a junk drawer.

Tents are a reasonable guess, but that's not what the text says. Obadiah hid the hundred prophets of the LORD fifty men per cave. Jezebel, Ahab's wife (1 Kings 16:31), had slaughtered other prophets of the LORD, so hiding mattered. He kept those prophets fed and watered, too.

explanations.answer: Grass to keep the horses and mules alive
explanations.explanation: Grass it is. Ahab says, "Perhaps we will find grass to keep the horses and mules alive so that we will not have to destroy any livestock." The famine is so severe that the king's animals are at risk. Even the king is out searching every spring and valley for something green.

explanations.answer: Grain to feed the hungry people of Samaria
explanations.explanation: Grain makes sense in a famine. But the text names something else. Ahab hopes to find grass to keep the horses and mules alive. His worry in this verse is about his animals, and the text says nothing here about grain.

explanations.answer: Water to fill up the palace wells again
explanations.explanation: Water sounds sensible when you hear the words spring and valley. But Ahab says what he's after: "…grass to keep the horses and mules alive…" The wells don't come up in his words. He's checking those spots for something green to feed his animals.

The text says otherwise. "So they divided the land to explore." Ahab went one way by himself, and Obadiah went the other way by himself. Two men, two directions, zero company. That detail matters in the next scene.

False, and the text is plain about it. They divided the land to explore. Ahab went one way by himself, and Obadiah went the other way by himself. No side by side here. Keep that in mind, because Obadiah ends up on his own when something surprising shows up.
True. When Obadiah recognizes Elijah, he falls facedown. Then he asks, "Is it you, my lord Elijah?" Obadiah calls him "my lord," and I think the facedown part says he was shocked.

The text says he does. When Obadiah recognized Elijah, he "fell facedown." He didn't just stop or wave. Then he asked, "Is it you, my lord Elijah?" I think that's a man who did not expect to meet him on that road.

It's the reverse. Elijah doesn't ask for any secret. He says, "Go tell your master, ‘Elijah is here!’…" Obadiah's master is Ahab, the king who has been searching for Elijah. So Elijah wants the king told.
False. Elijah tells Obadiah, "Go tell your master, ‘Elijah is here!’…" That's an announcement, not a secret. Elijah wants Ahab to hear it.

That's what Obadiah fears. He asks, "How have I sinned, that you are handing your servant over to Ahab to put me to death?" He's not worried about a scolding. In his mind, this message could cost him his life.

explanations.answer: Throw him out of the palace
explanations.explanation: Losing a job is bad, but Obadiah is afraid of something much worse. He says Elijah is handing him over to Ahab "…to put me to death?" Being thrown out of the palace never comes up in his words. This is no HR problem, friend.

explanations.answer: Send him off to search more
explanations.explanation: More searching is what Obadiah is already doing, but that isn't his fear. He says Elijah is handing him over to Ahab "…to put me to death?" Obadiah is afraid for his life, not his schedule. I'd be afraid too.

True. Obadiah says that when they said, "He is not here…" Ahab "…made that kingdom or nation swear that they had not found you." The king wasn't just asking around. He wanted that kingdom's oath, and that's how hard he searched.

The text says Ahab did make them swear. Obadiah reports that when a kingdom said, "He is not here…" Ahab "…made that kingdom or nation swear that they had not found you." A simple no wasn't enough for him. He wanted a sworn answer.

explanations.answer: The Spirit of the LORD may carry him off
explanations.explanation: Right, that's Obadiah's worry. He says, "I do not know where the Spirit of the LORD may carry you off when I leave you." Then he spells out the problem. If Ahab comes and doesn't find Elijah, "…he will kill me." So he's afraid of an empty spot where Elijah was supposed to be.

explanations.answer: Ahab's searchers may catch up to him first
explanations.explanation: Obadiah doesn't say that. His worry is about the Spirit of the LORD. He says, "I do not know where the Spirit of the LORD may carry you off when I leave you." If Elijah is gone when Ahab shows up, Obadiah says, "…he will kill me."

explanations.answer: He may slip back into hiding by the brook
explanations.explanation: Obadiah never mentions a brook. What he says is, "I do not know where the Spirit of the LORD may carry you off when I leave you." His fear is that Elijah will be gone when Ahab arrives. Then Obadiah says, "…he will kill me."

Today! Elijah says, "As surely as the LORD of Hosts lives, before whom I stand, I will present myself to Ahab today." That answers Obadiah's worry about Elijah vanishing (1 Kings 18:12). Elijah puts the LORD's life behind his word. I think that would settle my nerves a little.
Tomorrow would give Obadiah more time to worry. But Elijah says, "…I will present myself to Ahab today." He swears it by the LORD of Hosts, before whom he stands. No waiting around.

Eventually is a word for people who are not sure. Elijah says, "As surely as the LORD of Hosts lives, before whom I stand, I will present myself to Ahab today." He picks a day, and the day is today. I bet Obadiah was glad to hear it.

That's who Elijah names. He says, "I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father's house have…" He hands the title right back to the king. That's like someone handing you back a bill you were sure was theirs.
Elijah doesn't point at the people of Samaria. He says, "I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father's house have…" The "you" is Ahab himself. The blame goes to the king and his family.

Other kings never come up in Elijah's answer. He says, "I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father's house have…" He is talking straight to Ahab. The king and his father's house get the blame.

Commandments is right. Elijah says Ahab and his father's house "…have forsaken the commandments of the LORD…" That's the charge, and it's the real trouble he names. The king called Elijah the troubler, and Elijah answered with this.
Baals fits the second blank. Elijah says Ahab and his father's house "…have followed the Baals." The Baals are false gods. So they walked away from the LORD's commandments and followed those instead.
Temple doesn't fit here. Elijah says Ahab and his father's house have forsaken "…the commandments of the LORD…" The word temple isn't in what Elijah says. The charge is about the commandments.

The Egyptians don't come up in Elijah's charge. He says Ahab and his father's house have "…followed the Baals." The Baals are false gods, and that's who they followed. The people of Egypt aren't in this verse at all.
Levites are not in this verse. Elijah says Ahab and his father's house have "…followed the Baals." The Baals are false gods. Nobody here is blamed for following the Levites.

Mount Carmel is the spot. Elijah tells Ahab to summon all Israel to meet him on Mount Carmel. He also names who should come with them. The one who was being searched for is now picking the meeting place.

Mount Sinai is a famous mountain, and the LORD came down on it to call Moses, Israel's leader, up (Exodus 19:20). But Elijah doesn't name Sinai here. He tells Ahab to summon all Israel to Mount Carmel.
Mount Zion is a real mountain in the Bible (Psalm 48:2). It's just not the one Elijah picks. He tells Ahab to summon all Israel to meet him on Mount Carmel.

Jezebel's table. Elijah says the four hundred prophets of Asherah "…eat at Jezebel’s table." Jezebel is Ahab's wife (1 Kings 16:31). Elijah also names the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, but the table is mentioned with the prophets of Asherah.
Ahab is the king, so it's a fair guess. But Elijah says the prophets of Asherah "…eat at Jezebel’s table." Jezebel is Ahab's wife (1 Kings 16:31). Her name is the one Elijah uses.

Obadiah is the one who hid a hundred prophets of the LORD, so I see the mix-up. But the prophets Elijah mentions here are of Baal and Asherah. He says the prophets of Asherah "…eat at Jezebel’s table." Jezebel is Ahab's wife (1 Kings 16:31).
